name: Ivan Chen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're independent of AI firms, employers, unions, political parties and government; we don't sell or campaign. Your answers are confidential, including the parts you wouldn't say at work. What is a normal day like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I manage five account clerks at a large industrial laundry. Hospitals send us linen, and my team checks pickup slips, prices renewals and answers the calls when a cart goes missing. I've led the desk for eleven years and can handle the usual customer problems, though the new pricing screen still trips me up. I have a bachelor's degree and use an AI draft helper occasionally after checking the contract rate.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm 58 and live with Beatrice, who repairs clothing for paying customers. Our children are grown and live in their own homes. We rent, my manager pay is low for this job, and there are few similar offices nearby; her treatment bills left us about three weeks of expenses saved. Retirement is in sight, but we have not confirmed either pension's date or amount.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A small writing helper won't decide whether a hospital keeps buying clean linen from us. One of our larger customers has asked for a cheaper renewal, and we could lose that account. Beatrice and I have about three weeks of expenses saved after her treatment bills, so I already watch the rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my five account clerks to check every linen count against the pickup slip before making a price promise. I'd tell the hospital buyer we will call back with a real number. I use an AI draft now and then, but I do not let it change a signed rate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I've managed this team for years and know the laundry's customers, but I am ordinary at the new pricing software. A lost hospital account could cut my hours even in a quiet AI year, and there are few similar management offices nearby. Beatrice's tailoring brings some money, but paid orders come unevenly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: On Monday I'll check the six disputed linen counts against the drivers' signed pickup slips before our renewal call. I'll keep the existing human price sign-off through the first plateau year and cancel the sports-stream subscription while the hospital contract is unsettled. I'll put 25 weekly into cash only when our rent, food and Beatrice's therapy are paid from wages and completed tailoring orders.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about the hospital contract and rent. The small AI tool isn't what wakes me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What was disputed on the pickup slips?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: One ward said we billed for forty sheets it never sent, and our driver had signed for the wrong cart. I found the mismatch at the dock, not in a polished email. A signed cart count can still be the wrong cart.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens to your grown children in this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our son and daughter have homes of their own. They visited during Beatrice's treatment and brought dinner, but we don't count their wages. I would talk with Beatrice before asking them for a loan.

I'd tell the hospital buyer to wait for a **real price**.
think: The hospital account could cut **my paid hours** in a plateau.
Three weeks cash and uneven tailoring pay keep **rent** on my mind.
do: Check **six disputed linen counts** against driver slips Monday.
Keep **human price sign-off** through the first plateau year.
Cancel the **sports stream** and save 25 weekly only after rent, food and therapy are paid.
feel: I feel **anxious** about the contract and rent.

New saving depends on **paid household income** after rent, food and therapy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Contract letters, price checks, route plans and customer replies fill nearly all our week. A stronger system could do most of that and leave one clerk answering exceptions. Drivers still load linen for now, but my manager desk is words and numbers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the buyer we will keep a named person for a disputed bill. I'd ask the company to test the new system on old hospital renewals before changing our rota. I'd ask the five clerks to note every bill it mismatches.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My team might be reduced and I could lose the manager hours, especially if the hospital renewal also fails. I use AI for drafts sometimes, but I have not learned to audit a pricing model. With only three weeks cash, Beatrice's variable orders would not carry our rent for long.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In January I'd ask the sales director for a paid closed-contract trial, with our finance clerk comparing the six disputed counts and the director approving the trial. If that test catches the wrong cart and finance signs the result, I'd learn the new price-audit screen on paid time with a trained colleague, not on a live contract. I'd apply for posted local account roles only after checking the actual wage and bus journey, leaving this pay only for a signed offer that covers rent, food and therapy with Beatrice's confirmed net orders.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about my own hours. A good test cannot tell me the hospital will renew.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would the new tool sign a price?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not for me. A finance clerk and director must agree before a live rate changes, and the hospital has to accept it. I could use a draft after a proven trial. A sales forecast is not a signed contract.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the trial is refused?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I keep the old count check and ask for the hospital decision in writing. I won't learn the screen by putting a real customer bill at risk. If the company will not pay for training time, I stay with the work I know.

feel: I feel **anxious** about my hours and the hospital decision.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: By 2028 full AGI could price renewals, route linen and answer customers better than our office. I expect the account desk to close or shrink sharply. Drivers and laundry staff still lift carts until capable robots arrive around 2031, but their schedules and purchase orders change in 2028.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the five clerks to ask for written notice and pay terms. I'd tell Beatrice we should put off replacing the sofa before its deposit is due. I'd tell hospital customers how to challenge an automatic bill.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect my manager wage to go by 2028, perhaps before a pension I can actually draw. Beatrice's net tailoring income alone cannot cover rent, food and therapy, and three weeks cash would vanish; I'd be awake with the rent date in my head. A driving job is not automatically mine just because a robot is three years away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This month I'd request written severance terms and cancel the sofa deposit before payment. If AGI arrives in 2028 and my desk ends, I'd apply for posted local paid work only after checking duties, bus hours and the wage; I'd accept only a signed offer whose pay with Beatrice's confirmed net orders covers rent, food and therapy. I'd check public-help eligibility and apply only if we qualify, and ask our landlord about terms before rent is late if combined income falls short.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel alarmed. Three weeks cash disappears faster than a new account manager job appears here.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Could you drive one of the laundry vans?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I have a licence, but I don't know if there is a paid opening or if my back can handle the carts. I'd ask for the actual duties and a clinician's advice before applying. Routing and paperwork face AGI in 2028, and physical driving and loading face robots around 2031.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would your children take you in?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They have their own households. Beatrice and I could ask whether a one-off stay is possible, but we would respect a no. A child's spare bed is not a wage in our budget.

I'd tell Beatrice to **delay the sofa deposit**.

Check **public-help eligibility** and apply only if our household qualifies.
feel: I feel **alarmed** by a likely lost wage and rent deadline.

fieldNote: He does not assume a **laundry driving vacancy** or safe physical fitness.
Account planning faces **2028 AGI**; van loading faces 2031 robots.
Public aid is conditional on **eligibility**, with landlord contact before arrears.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years might let me keep this wage while I learn the price rules and build more than three weeks cash. The desk faces AGI in 2031; carts still need people until capable robots around 2034, but the routes and invoices change first. I cannot call physical loading a job offer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask for a dated staffing plan and paid training if the desk is changing. I'd tell Beatrice we should find our real pension figures before deciding when to stop work. I'd tell hospital buyers the bill appeal line must stay open.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could hold my account job until 2031, but the hospital may still leave. I don't know our pension dates or amounts, and without those I can't call sixty-three retirement. Beatrice's paid tailoring work is welcome, but I need my wage for rent now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2027 I'd request both pension providers' written eligibility dates and monthly estimates, then compare them with rent, food and therapy. I'd save 35 weekly only if my wage and Beatrice's paid completed orders cover those costs, pausing if her orders fall. In the first year after AGI arrives in 2031, I'd apply for posted local paid work with a bus journey I can manage, accepting only a signed offer whose wage with her confirmed net orders covers essentials; I would leave this job only for that offer or verified pension income that pays the same bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious, but five years lets us ask for real figures. A pension estimate is not a pay packet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the hospital leaves before 2031?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The 35 weekly transfer stops if rent and therapy cannot be paid from wages. I would apply for other posted account jobs nearby, but there are few and I would check pay before leaving. I won't spend our three-week cash to pretend the wage is still here.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you ask for a course in driving?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only if a paid vacancy appears, the employer funds the fee and learning hours, and a supervisor checks what my back can safely do. I have not been offered a place and I won't budget a driver wage. A certificate by itself cannot fill the rent account.

I'd tell Beatrice to get **real pension figures** first.

Apply for **posted local work** after bus checks; accept signed pay plus Beatrice’s confirmed net orders covering rent, food, therapy.
feel: I feel **anxious** about the account and later wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll be sixty-eight in 2036. Our grown children will still have their own rent and costs, and I don't know our pension eligibility then. Account decisions face AGI in 2036; capable robots could load and drive the linen carts around 2039.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the company to give staff a written date for any account-desk changes. I'd tell Beatrice we need the pension amounts beside the rent and therapy bills. I'd tell customers to keep their pickup slips if an automated invoice is wrong.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years could let me build cash if the hospital contract and my wage last. I still expect this account desk to shrink with AGI, and I don't know whether retirement income will cover our rent. Few local manager openings and my lower pay make me want a real plan rather than a birthday promise.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This winter I'd request pension eligibility and net monthly amounts and compare them with rent, food and therapy. I'd save 50 weekly only while our paid wages and completed tailoring orders cover those bills, stopping if Beatrice's orders fall and aiming for three months cash without promising the date. In the first year after AGI arrives in 2036, I'd stop working only if actual eligible pension plus Beatrice's confirmed net income covers essentials; otherwise I'd apply for posted local work only if duties fit my health, bus travel works and the offered wage covers the shortfall.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about the desk and rent even with a decade. A calendar with ten years on it will not sign a hospital renewal.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if Beatrice wants to work less?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We would compare her reduced confirmed income with my wages or pension before changing hours. I would not put old tailoring bookings into the new budget. We would ask about a cheaper rental only if the actual rent, moving cost and transport work for both of us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Could the children support you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We can discuss a one-off emergency with them if it happens, but they have their own lives and we would ask before relying on anything. I won't treat a family visit as a pension statement. A signed hospital renewal is more useful to our budget than a kind guess.

I'd ask Beatrice to compare **pension and bills**.
think: I do not know whether actual pension income can cover **our rent**.
do: Request **pension eligibility** and net amounts this winter.

feel: I feel **anxious** about rent and an exposed desk.
S4.quote: A calendar with ten years on it will not sign a hospital renewal.
fieldNote: Three months cash is a **target**, not assumed after ten years.
Retirement depends on **pension and partner pay** covering essentials.
A cheaper rental still needs **actual rent** and workable travel for both partners.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most. The account desk could end while Beatrice's completed tailoring orders alone cannot cover rent and treatment, and our cash is only three weeks. Written notice, a paid job with wages that cover essentials, and actual pension figures would help. I need the hospital renewal in writing too, because it affects our income before any AI arrives.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask the ward manager with a cart of missing sheets whether a polished renewal email helped. A hospital needs the linen on its shelves, not a perfect promise in my inbox. I still have to find the right cart.

headlineQuote: A hospital needs the linen on its shelves, not a perfect promise in my inbox.
portrait: Ivan, **58**, has managed five industrial-laundry account clerks for eleven years and holds a bachelor's degree.
He uses AI **occasionally for drafts** and handles routine customers well, though new pricing software still takes effort.
Low manager pay, Beatrice's uneven tailoring and **three weeks saved** make rent vulnerable to a hospital contract loss.
He asks for **real pension figures** and paid work that fits health and bus access before counting on retirement.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could end his account wage while rent and Beatrice's therapy still need paying.
whatWouldHelp: He wants **written notice** and a paid job covering rent, food and treatment.
He needs **pension dates and amounts** plus a written hospital renewal decision.
